entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) emerged from the Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation, signed on December 7, 1944, in Chicago, Illinois. This pivotal agreement brought together 52 nations, establishing a framework for international air travel regulations and ensuring the safety of civil aviation. ICAO plays a critical role in the global economy and international relations by setting standards that govern the operation of civil aviation globally. Key figures in its establishment include Dr. Albert Picard, the first Secretary General, and various national representatives who recognized the need for a unified approach to air transport post-World War II.

Following its inception, ICAO set about creating a comprehensive set of standards and recommended practices, known as Annexes, which cover various aspects of aviation operations. By 1947, the organization had established the International Air Transport Association (IATA) to facilitate cooperation among airlines. Throughout the years, ICAO has been instrumental in significant events such as the establishment of safety protocols following numerous aviation disasters and the promotion of sustainable aviation practices in response to climate change concerns. The organization has also facilitated the growth of international air traffic, which has soared from 8 million passengers in 1945 to over 4 billion in 2019, highlighting the significance of air travel in today's interconnected world.
